stem: A 27-year-old man with Crohn disease has had 3 weeks of crampy abdominal pain, diarrhea and drainage from a perianal fistula. He is started on ciprofloxacin, metronidazole and prednisone, and his symptoms improve over the next 10 days.
oneliner: 27M + Crohn disease flare + perianal fistula + ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, prednisone + improves in 10 d → which mechanism explains the prednisone effect?
ask: Which of the following best explains the benefit of prednisone in this disease?

options.D: Suppressing T-lymphocyte activation and cytokine release

whyNot.A: That is **cromolyn**; not how steroids work in Crohn disease
whyNot.B: Not the main steroid effect; **complement** is not the target here
whyNot.E: Steroids **impair** neutrophil function and do not enhance killing

answer: Suppression of T-lymphocyte function and cytokine production
why: **Crohn disease is driven by T-cell cytokines.** **Glucocorticoids suppress T-cell activation and cytokine release** (IL-2, TNF, others), which is why prednisone helps a flare.

drug.name: Prednisone
drug.how: Binds the cytosolic receptor and alters gene transcription: less cytokine production and T-cell activity
drug.use: Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis flares, autoimmune disease, asthma
drug.watch: Hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, cushingoid features, infection risk, adrenal suppression

chain: T-cell activation and gut inflammation fall

stem: A 30-year-old woman develops an intensely itchy linear streak of vesicles on her forearm 2 days after clearing brush in her garden. Her physician diagnoses allergic contact dermatitis from poison ivy and prescribes a topical hydrocortisone analog cream.
oneliner: 30F + itchy linear vesicles on forearm 2 d after gardening + poison ivy dermatitis + topical hydrocortisone analog → which step in arachidonic acid production does it block?
ask: The cream reduces inflammation mainly by which of the following effects?

whyNot.B: That is how **NSAIDs** work, and it leaves the leukotriene pathway intact
whyNot.E: Would **raise** inflammatory products, not lower them

why: **Corticosteroids induce lipocortin**, which **inhibits phospholipase A2**, so less arachidonic acid is released and both **prostaglandins and leukotrienes** fall.

drug.name: Corticosteroids (hydrocortisone)
drug.how: Induce lipocortin, which inhibits phospholipase A2; also alter gene transcription
drug.use: Contact dermatitis, eczema, asthma, autoimmune disease, adrenal insufficiency
drug.watch: Topical: skin atrophy and striae; systemic: hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, infection risk

stem: A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has new edema, hypertension and heavy proteinuria. Kidney biopsy shows diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis, and she is started on high-dose prednisone. A student asks where in the cell the drug acts.
oneliner: 28F + lupus + edema, hypertension, heavy proteinuria + diffuse proliferative nephritis + high-dose prednisone → where and how does it act?
ask: Which of the following best describes how the drug acts in cells?

options.A: Binding a cell-surface receptor with tyrosine kinase activity
options.B: Binding a cytosolic receptor that moves to the nucleus and changes gene transcription
options.C: Binding a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP
options.E: Binding a receptor on mitochondria that alters respiration

whyNot.A: That is the pathway of **insulin and growth factors**
whyNot.C: That is the pathway of **beta-agonists and glucagon**
whyNot.D: That is the pathway of **benzodiazepines and acetylcholine**
whyNot.E: Steroid receptors are not on mitochondria

answer: Cytosolic receptor that moves to the nucleus and alters gene transcription
why: **Prednisone is lipid-soluble**, crosses the cell membrane, binds a **cytosolic glucocorticoid receptor**, and the complex **moves to the nucleus** to change gene transcription.

drug.name: Prednisone
drug.how: Binds the cytosolic receptor; the complex moves to the nucleus and changes gene transcription
drug.use: Lupus nephritis, autoimmune disease, asthma, transplant, adrenal insufficiency
drug.watch: Hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, cushingoid features, infection risk, adrenal suppression

stem: A 42-year-old man with severe asthma receives a single dose of dexamethasone. Its plasma half-life is about 4 hours, but his airway inflammation stays suppressed for more than 2 days. His physician asks why the effect lasts so much longer than the drug stays in blood.
oneliner: 42M + severe asthma + single dose of dexamethasone + plasma half-life 4 h + anti-inflammatory effect lasts over 2 days → why does the effect outlast the drug?
ask: Which of the following best explains this?

options.C: Receptor-induced synthesis of proteins that remain active after the drug is cleared
options.D: Active metabolites that accumulate in fat
options.E: Slow release from an intramuscular depot

whyNot.A: Protein binding affects **free drug level** in blood, not the length of cell effects
whyNot.D: **Fat storage** is not the explanation for a single dose
whyNot.E: He received a **single dose**, not a depot injection

answer: Receptor-induced proteins that persist after drug is gone
why: Glucocorticoids act through **gene transcription**: the receptor makes **new proteins** that keep working after the drug is gone, so **biologic effect outlasts plasma half-life**.

drug.name: Dexamethasone
drug.how: Binds the cytosolic receptor and alters gene transcription; induced proteins persist
drug.use: Cerebral edema, antiemetic, adrenal suppression testing, antenatal lung maturity, severe inflammation
drug.watch: Hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, cushingoid features, infection risk, adrenal suppression

stem: A 46-year-old man receives a liver transplant for alcoholic cirrhosis. After surgery he is started on cyclosporine to prevent rejection. A resident is asked to explain how the drug stops T cells from attacking the graft.
oneliner: 46M + liver transplant for cirrhosis + started on cyclosporine for rejection prevention → how does it work?
ask: Cyclosporine prevents rejection mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.B: Blocking purine synthesis in proliferating B cells
options.C: Inhibiting mTOR to block IL-2 receptor signaling
options.D: Binding cyclophilin to inhibit calcineurin and IL-2 gene transcription
options.E: Blocking the IL-2 receptor alpha chain

whyNot.A: Would **increase** IL-2 production and worsen rejection
whyNot.C: **Sirolimus**: acts after IL-2 binds; does not stop IL-2 production
whyNot.E: **Basiliximab**: an antibody that blocks IL-2 action, not its synthesis

answer: Cyclophilin-cyclosporine complex blocks calcineurin, so IL-2 synthesis falls
why: **Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin**, the complex **inhibits calcineurin**, so **NFAT stays phosphorylated** and **IL-2 and other cytokine genes are not transcribed**.

drug.name: Cyclosporine / tacrolimus
drug.how: Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin; tacrolimus binds FKBP12; both inhibit calcineurin and IL-2 transcription
drug.watch: Nephrotoxicity, hypertension, tremor, hyperglycemia (tacrolimus), gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism (cyclosporine)

stem: A 52-year-old woman with severe keratoconjunctivitis sicca is enrolled in a trial of an experimental systemic LFA-1 antagonist. Compared with placebo, participants on the drug develop more bacterial skin and respiratory infections. Biopsies of infected sites show few neutrophils despite a high blood neutrophil count.
oneliner: 52F + dry eye trial of a systemic LFA-1 antagonist + more bacterial infections + few neutrophils in tissue, high blood neutrophils → which step of neutrophil recruitment is impaired?
ask: Which step of neutrophil recruitment is most directly impaired by this drug?
answer: Firm adhesion (LFA-1 binds ICAM-1) is lost
why: **Neutrophils are in the blood but not in tissue** because **LFA-1 binding to ICAM-1** (firm adhesion) is blocked. **Selectins** handle rolling, which is unaffected.

drug.name: Lifitegrast
drug.how: Blocks LFA-1 binding to ICAM-1, reducing T-cell adhesion and inflammation
drug.watch: Eye irritation, altered taste, reduced visual acuity

stem: A 45-year-old man is 3 weeks past a kidney transplant. Creatinine has risen and biopsy shows acute cellular rejection with lymphocytic tubulitis. The rejection persists after pulse methylprednisolone, so he is given a murine monoclonal antibody that binds a component on T cells and removes them from the circulation.
oneliner: 45M + kidney transplant 3 wk + acute cellular rejection + persists after pulse steroids + murine monoclonal antibody binds T cells → what does it bind?
ask: The antibody most likely binds which of the following targets?

options.A: Alpha chain of the IL-2 receptor (CD25)
options.E: Epsilon chain of CD3 in the T-cell receptor complex

whyNot.A: **Basiliximab** target; a chimeric antibody, not murine
whyNot.B: **Infliximab and adalimumab** target; not for steroid-resistant rejection
whyNot.C: **Rituximab** target; B cells, not T cells

answer: CD3 epsilon chain of the T-cell receptor complex (muromonab-CD3)
why: **Steroid-resistant rejection treated with a murine anti-T-cell antibody** = **muromonab-CD3 (OKT3)**. It binds the **epsilon chain of CD3** on the TCR complex and causes **cytokine release** on first doses.

drug.name: Muromonab-CD3 (OKT3)
drug.how: Binds the CD3 epsilon chain of the T-cell receptor complex, blocking T-cell function
drug.watch: Cytokine release syndrome, anti-mouse antibodies, pulmonary edema

chain: Binds CD3 epsilon on T cells
TCR signaling blocked, T cells cleared

stem: A 40-year-old woman who had a kidney transplant 2 months ago takes prednisone and an oral immunosuppressant that is a prodrug and is toxic to rapidly dividing cells. Her white cell count is slightly low, and her physician reminds her not to take allopurinol without checking first.
oneliner: 40F + kidney transplant 2 mo + prednisone + oral prodrug immunosuppressant toxic to dividing cells + slightly low WBC + allopurinol warning → how does the drug work?
ask: The immunosuppressant works mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.C: Conversion to a purine analog that blocks nucleic acid synthesis

whyNot.E: **Basiliximab** mechanism; an injected antibody, not an oral drug

why: **Azathioprine** is converted to **6-mercaptopurine**, a **purine antagonist** that blocks DNA and RNA synthesis in dividing lymphocytes. **Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor)** raises its levels and toxicity.

drug.name: Azathioprine
drug.how: Converted to 6-MP; blocks purine synthesis in dividing lymphocytes
drug.use: Transplant rejection prophylaxis, IBD, autoimmune disease
drug.watch: Myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity; toxic with allopurinol (give less); check TPMT

stem: A 28-year-old man has had low back pain and morning stiffness for 18 months that improves with exercise. Imaging shows bilateral sacroiliitis and he is HLA-B27 positive. Symptoms persist despite two different NSAIDs at full dose and a 3-month trial of sulfasalazine. His physician recommends the next step.
oneliner: 28M + 18 mo low back pain, morning stiffness better with exercise + bilateral sacroiliitis + HLA-B27+ + failed NSAIDs and sulfasalazine → how does the next drug work?
ask: The most appropriate next drug works by which of the following mechanisms?
why: **Ankylosing spondylitis refractory to NSAIDs and sulfasalazine** responds to **TNF-alpha inhibitors** (**adalimumab, infliximab, etanercept**).

drug.name: Adalimumab / infliximab
drug.use: Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis, Crohn disease
drug.watch: Reactivation of latent TB, serious infections, lymphoma; screen for TB and hepatitis B before starting

stem: A 57-year-old man has metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma with multiple lung nodules. He receives high-dose recombinant interleukin-2 in hospital. Three months later a CT scan shows that the lung nodules have shrunk markedly.
oneliner: 57M + metastatic clear cell RCC to lung + high-dose IL-2 → nodules shrink in 3 mo → how?
ask: Which of the following best explains the tumor response?

options.A: Direct killing of tumor cells by interleukin-2
options.B: Production of antitumor antibodies by plasma cells
options.C: Increased natural killer and cytotoxic T-cell activity
options.E: Blockade of PD-1 on T cells

whyNot.A: **A cytokine** signals through receptors on immune cells; it is not itself cytotoxic
whyNot.B: **B-cell** antibody effects are not the main action of IL-2
whyNot.D: **Anti-VEGF drugs** (sunitinib, bevacizumab) are different agents from IL-2
whyNot.E: **Checkpoint inhibitors** (nivolumab) are different agents from IL-2

answer: Increased natural killer and cytotoxic T-cell activity
why: **Recombinant IL-2** stimulates **T-cell and natural killer cell growth and cytotoxicity**, so the immune system attacks the tumor.

drug.name: Aldesleukin (recombinant IL-2)
drug.how: Stimulates growth and activation of T cells and NK cells
drug.use: Metastatic renal cell carcinoma, metastatic melanoma
drug.watch: Capillary leak syndrome with hypotension and pulmonary edema

chain: Binds IL-2 receptor on T and NK cells
T and NK cells multiply and activate

stem: A 44-year-old man, 6 months after a kidney transplant, is switched from his usual immunosuppressant to a drug that binds FK-binding protein. His T cells still make IL-2 normally, but they fail to divide when IL-2 binds its receptor.
oneliner: 44M + kidney transplant + switched to FK-binding-protein-binding drug + IL-2 still made + T cells do not proliferate to IL-2 → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism of action best explains this drug's effect?

options.D: Binding CD3 on the T-cell receptor

whyNot.A: **IL-2 is still made** here; calcineurin block (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) stops IL-2 transcription
whyNot.B: That is **mycophenolate**: blocks purine synthesis in lymphocytes, does not bind FKBP
whyNot.D: That is **muromonab-CD3**, a surface antibody, not a small drug bound to FKBP
whyNot.E: That is **azathioprine**; it does not bind FK-binding protein

answer: mTOR inhibition (sirolimus): blocks T-cell proliferation in response to IL-2
why: Sirolimus binds **FK-binding protein** like tacrolimus, but the complex inhibits **mTOR**, not calcineurin. **IL-2 is still produced**; the T cell cannot respond to it and stops dividing.

idea.rule: Same binding protein, different target: the target decides whether IL-2 production or IL-2 response is blocked.
also: Tacrolimus: FKBP complex inhibits calcineurin (IL-2 transcription falls)
Cyclosporine: cyclophilin complex inhibits calcineurin
Basiliximab: blocks CD25, the IL-2 receptor alpha chain
Sirolimus also helps prevent coronary stent restenosis (drug-eluting stents)

drug.name: Sirolimus (rapamycin)
drug.how: Binds FKBP; the complex inhibits mTOR, so T cells cannot proliferate in response to IL-2
drug.use: Kidney transplant rejection prophylaxis; drug-eluting coronary stents
drug.watch: Hyperlipidemia, thrombocytopenia, poor wound healing; not nephrotoxic

stem: A 52-year-old man after liver transplantation takes tacrolimus. In the laboratory, his activated T cells show NFAT that stays phosphorylated and a fall in IL-2 transcription, as with cyclosporine. The drug, however, binds a different intracellular protein than cyclosporine does.
oneliner: 52M + liver transplant + tacrolimus + NFAT stays phosphorylated + IL-2 transcription falls + binds a different protein than cyclosporine → which protein?
ask: To which intracellular protein does this drug bind?

whyNot.A: This is the protein **cyclosporine** binds; the stem says it differs
whyNot.B: mTOR is the **target of sirolimus** (after FKBP binding), not the binding protein, and NFAT would not stay phosphorylated
whyNot.C: Target of **basiliximab**; an antibody on the cell surface, not an intracellular protein
whyNot.D: Target of **mycophenolate**, which acts on purine synthesis

answer: FK-binding protein; the complex inhibits calcineurin
why: Tacrolimus and cyclosporine both end in **calcineurin inhibition**, so **NFAT stays phosphorylated** and IL-2 is not made. They differ in the first step: tacrolimus binds **FK-binding protein**, cyclosporine binds **cyclophilin**.

idea.rule: Two drugs, one target: tacrolimus (FKBP) and cyclosporine (cyclophilin) both block calcineurin.
also: Cyclosporine: gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, nephrotoxicity
Tacrolimus: nephrotoxicity, hyperglycemia, neurotoxicity
Sirolimus uses FKBP too but inhibits mTOR
Both are CYP3A4 substrates

drug.name: Tacrolimus
drug.how: Binds FKBP; the complex inhibits calcineurin, so NFAT stays phosphorylated and IL-2 transcription falls
drug.watch: Nephrotoxicity, hypertension, neurotoxicity, hyperglycemia; no gingival hyperplasia or hirsutism

stem: A 27-year-old woman is stung by a bee and 20 minutes later has generalized hives, audible wheeze and a blood pressure of 78/44 mm Hg. Intramuscular epinephrine is given; within minutes her pressure rises and the wheeze settles.
oneliner: 27F + bee sting 20 min ago + hives + wheeze + BP 78/44 + IM epinephrine → BP up and wheeze settles in minutes → which receptors does it act on?
ask: Through which set of receptors does epinephrine reverse both her shock and her bronchospasm?

whyNot.B: Norepinephrine-like: raises pressure but has little **beta-2**, so her **wheeze** would not settle
whyNot.C: Isoproterenol-like: without **alpha-1**, beta-2 vasodilation would lower her **pressure of 78/44** further
whyNot.D: Phenylephrine-like: lifts pressure but does nothing for the **wheeze**
whyNot.E: Albuterol-like: eases the **wheeze** but dilates muscle arterioles, so the **shock** persists

answer: Alpha-1 (vasoconstriction), beta-1 (heart rate and contractility) and beta-2 (bronchodilation)
why: Anaphylaxis drops pressure through **mediator-driven vasodilation and leak** and narrows the airways. Epinephrine's **alpha-1** action constricts arterioles, **beta-1** supports heart rate and contractility, and **beta-2** opens the bronchi and damps further mast-cell release; no single receptor does all of this.

idea.rule: Epinephrine works against anaphylaxis at three receptors: alpha-1 (pressure), beta-1 (heart), beta-2 (airway).
also: Beta-2 also raises mast-cell cAMP and reduces further mediator release
Norepinephrine is mostly alpha-1 and beta-1, with little beta-2
Antihistamines and steroids are add-ons, not rescue
Glucagon helps patients on beta-blockers who do not respond

drug.name: Epinephrine
drug.how: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction, beta-1 raises heart rate and contractility, beta-2 bronchodilation and less mast cell mediator release

stem: An investigator coats CD20-positive lymphoma cells with rituximab and adds lymphocytes that are CD3-negative and CD56-positive, with no complement in the dish. The tumor cells are lysed, and killing does not depend on MHC molecules on the targets.
oneliner: Experiment: rituximab-coated CD20+ lymphoma cells + CD3-negative CD56-positive lymphocytes, no complement → lysis, no MHC needed → which killer-cell receptor?
ask: Which receptor on the killer cells recognizes the antibody-coated targets?

options.B: CD16 binding the Fc portion of IgG

whyNot.A: Cytotoxic **T-cell** mechanism needing CD3 and MHC; these killers are **CD3-negative** and MHC-independent
whyNot.C: A **costimulatory** signal for T-cell activation, and these cells are **CD3-negative**
whyNot.D: **T helper to B cell** signal for class switching, not killing of coated targets
whyNot.E: A **complement** receptor on B cells (also the EBV receptor); **no complement** is present here

answer: CD16 (FcγRIII): antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity by NK cells
why: **CD3-negative, CD56-positive** lymphocytes are **NK cells**. They bind the Fc region of the bound IgG1 (rituximab) through **CD16** and release perforin and granzymes: **ADCC**, with no MHC restriction. This is one of the ways rituximab kills B cells, alongside complement.

idea.rule: NK cells kill in two ways: missing self (no MHC I) and antibody-coated targets (CD16, ADCC).
also: Rituximab also kills by complement-dependent cytotoxicity
Trastuzumab and cetuximab use NK-cell ADCC too
Tumor cells that lose MHC I are killed by NK cells, not CD8 T cells
Perforin and granzymes trigger target apoptosis

drug.name: Rituximab
drug.how: Coats CD20-positive B cells; NK cells bind its Fc via CD16 and kill them (ADCC); also complement-mediated lysis
drug.use: B-cell lymphoma, CLL, rheumatoid arthritis, ANCA vasculitis
drug.watch: Infusion reactions, hepatitis B reactivation, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

stem: A 26-year-old woman has itchy, watery eyes every spring. An over-the-counter oral antihistamine relieves the itch and tearing within an hour. The drug acts at one step of the allergic response.
oneliner: 26F + seasonal itchy watery eyes + relieved by oral antihistamine → which step does the drug block?
ask: Which step in the allergic response does this drug block?

options.A: IgE binding to FcεRI on mast cells

whyNot.B: Cromolyn **stabilizes mast cells**; antihistamines act after the histamine is released
whyNot.C: Blocked by **zileuton**; antihistamines leave leukotrienes untouched
whyNot.D: Blocked by **mepolizumab**; late-phase step, not the itch within an hour

answer: Blocks histamine at H1 receptors, reducing venular permeability, itch and tearing
why: The drug is a **receptor antagonist**: histamine is still released but cannot act on **H1 receptors**, so **venular leak, itch and tearing** ease. Earlier steps (IgE binding, degranulation) go on as before.

idea.rule: Antihistamines block the effector, not the trigger: they stop histamine acting, not its release.
also: Omalizumab blocks IgE
Cromolyn prevents mast-cell degranulation
Montelukast blocks cysteinyl leukotriene receptors
First-generation H1 blockers cause sedation and anticholinergic effects

drug.name: Oral H1 antihistamines (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine)
drug.how: Block histamine at H1 receptors, reducing venular leak, itch and tearing
drug.watch: Little sedation; first-generation agents sedate and have anticholinergic effects

stem: A 38-year-old man with ulcerative colitis takes prednisone. A study of his activated macrophages shows reduced mRNA for IL-1, TNF and COX-2. The drug acts through an intracellular receptor that moves to the nucleus.
oneliner: 38M + ulcerative colitis + prednisone + macrophages show less IL-1, TNF and COX-2 mRNA + intracellular receptor → which transcription factor is inhibited?
ask: Which transcription factor does the drug-receptor complex inhibit?

whyNot.A: Signals downstream of **IL-6 and JAK**; not the switch for COX-2 and TNF here
whyNot.B: The **calcineurin** target in T cells (IL-2); the stem describes **macrophage** IL-1, TNF and COX-2
whyNot.D: Driven by **cAMP and PKA**; not the glucocorticoid-receptor pathway
whyNot.E: A nuclear receptor **activated** by thiazolidinediones; not the inflammatory switch the steroid turns off

answer: Inhibition of NF-κB, lowering transcription of inflammatory cytokines and COX-2
why: The glucocorticoid-receptor complex enters the nucleus and **inhibits NF-κB**. Transcription of **IL-1, TNF and COX-2** falls, which explains the broad anti-inflammatory effect.

idea.rule: Glucocorticoids switch off inflammatory genes (NF-κB) and also switch on lipocortin, which inhibits phospholipase A2.
also: Less phospholipase A2 activity, so less arachidonic acid
Less IL-2 and fewer lymphocytes
Fewer eosinophils (apoptosis)
Neutrophils rise from demargination

drug.name: Prednisone
drug.how: Glucocorticoid receptor inhibits NF-kB, lowering transcription of IL-1, TNF and COX-2; also inhibits phospholipase A2
drug.use: Inflammatory and autoimmune disease, asthma, transplant rejection
drug.watch: Cushing features, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression, infection
